vignette:
A 19-month-old boy was brought to the emergency department after an episode of reduced consciousness while bathing. His parents reported that when lukewarm water was poured over his chest, he turned blue around the lips and began gasping for air. During this time, his eyes “rolled back,” and he did not interact with his parents. There were no clonic movements, and he did not respond to physical stimulation. He subsequently fell asleep for approximately 1 hour and was brought to the ED.

On arrival, he was alert and appeared well. There were no focal findings on examination, his development was appropriate, and laboratory studies—including a blood glucose level of 5.5 mmol/L—were normal. His parents reported similar, less profound episodes during bathing over the previous 2 weeks, in which his head would go back, his eyes would roll upward, and he would become floppy and limp for 2–3 minutes, followed by sleepiness. These episodes occurred only during bathing; contact with water in other settings did not provoke symptoms. He had normal developmental milestones and no significant past medical or family history.

An electrocardiogram demonstrated sinus rhythm with a normal QT interval. Bathing in lukewarm water while his vital signs were monitored provoked hypotonia, tachycardia, and brief apnea with associated desaturation. He stared straight ahead and made mouthing movements; he was removed from the bath, given high-flow oxygen, and again slept for about 1 hour. A further similar episode occurred later while he was sleeping, without any provocation. The first interictal EEG was normal using the standard 10–20 system. Because he was clinically well between episodes and there was an avoidable trigger, he was discharged with plans for follow-up investigations, including a brain MRI, a bathing EEG, and outpatient review.

vignette:
A 57-year-old woman was referred to our hospital 8 years after a partial resection of a presumed benign hepatic lesion and multiple sessions of transcatheter arterial embolization (TAE) for hemobilia from a right‐lobe tumor. She had experienced six episodes of hemobilia treated with TAE but had progressive enlargement of the right‐lobe mass. 

Her medical history included appendectomy, two Cesarean sections, and lobectomy for lung adenocarcinomas at age 53. She had no history of liver disease, including hepatolithiasis. 

On admission, vital signs were stable. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 11.1 g/dL; total bilirubin 0.5 mg/dL; AST 65 IU/L; ALT 54 IU/L; alkaline phosphatase 819 IU/L; γ-GTP 227 IU/L. Alpha-fetoprotein and PIVKA-II were within normal limits, while CEA was 12.8 ng/mL and CA19-9 was 862 U/mL. Viral hepatitis markers were negative. Physical examination revealed a liver edge palpable four fingerbreadths below the xiphoid process.

Abdominal ultrasonography showed a 10 × 15 cm multilocular oval mass with papillary infoldings in the right hepatic lobe. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a 15 cm low-density hepatic tumor occupying the right and caudal lobes, compressing the portal vein, with contrast-enhanced mural nodules. T1-weighted MRI revealed a low-intensity mass except for the nodules, which were hyperintense on T2-weighted images. Superior mesenteric arteriography showed the right hepatic artery arising from the SMA with tumor staining. FDG-PET/CT showed intense uptake in the lesion. 

Endoscopic retrograde cholangiography demonstrated obstruction of the right hepatic bile duct, compression of the left hepatic duct, and dilation of peripheral bile ducts. The cystic lesion was suspected to be a mucin-producing biliary tumor, such as a mucinous cystic neoplasm of the liver or an intraductal papillary neoplasm of the bile duct. Biliary cytology revealed papillary adenocarcinoma in situ or papillary adenoma with severe atypia.

vignette:
A 19-year-old woman presented with an 18-month history of pain in the plantar aspect of her left foot.  The pain was moderate initially, often worse at night, and markedly exacerbated by compression and exposure to cold.  Over the past four months, the patient noted aggravation of the local pain and was referred for imaging.  She denied any trauma and had no family history of neurofibromatosis.  

On examination, three prominent, soft-tissue nodules with swelling and tenderness were palpated in the plantar aspect of the left foot; they were mobile and not adherent to surrounding tissue.  Sensation testing revealed numbness in the medial distal plantar foot; toe and foot motor strength were normal.  

Magnetic resonance imaging of the left foot demonstrated three nodules arranged in a linear distribution in the mid-plantar region.  On T1-weighted images, the lesions were homogeneously isointense to skeletal muscle.  On T2-weighted fat-suppressed images, they were homogeneously hyperintense without cystic degeneration; each was surrounded by a hyperintense rim.  A small extension of high signal from the lateral aspect of one lesion resembled a “mouse-tail.”  Two nodules were located within the flexor digitorum brevis muscle beneath the plantar aponeurosis, and one was in the superficial fascia at the third metatarsophalangeal joint.  The lesions followed the course of branches of the common plantar digital nerves without evidence of invasion.  

Based on the clinical presentation and imaging findings, the differential diagnosis included glomus tumor, neurofibroma, and schwannoma.  Multiple plexiform schwannoma was suspected, and surgical excision was recommended.

vignette:
A 55-year-old woman presented with generalized gum bleeding and halitosis. Her medical history was noncontributory, and she had undergone orthodontic treatment 18 years earlier. Extraoral examination was unremarkable. Intraorally, there was generalized bleeding on probing and clinical attachment loss; radiographs showed generalized alveolar bone loss consistent with stage II, grade II periodontitis. Periapical radiographs of the maxillary central incisors revealed cervical areas of rarefaction. On endodontic evaluation, both central incisors were normal in color, responded normally to cold testing, and were asymptomatic to percussion and palpation. A 5 mm probing depth was recorded on the palatal aspects of both teeth. Two additional periapical radiographs with mesial and distal angulation showed that the lesion’s projection remained in the same position relative to the canal and that the canal outline was undisturbed. Cone-beam computed tomography demonstrated radiolucent resorptive lesions cervically on the palatal aspects of teeth #11 and #21, originating from the external palatal surface and perforating into the pulp space. The diagnosis for both central incisors was asymptomatic irreversible pulpitis with normal apical tissues and external cervical resorption.

vignette:
A 34-year-old Filipino man presented with a 4-month history of left eye proptosis, diplopia, and chemosis without epistaxis, headache, or nasal obstruction. Endoscopic nasal examination revealed a mass at the level of the left middle turbinate extending into the left nasal roof and eroding the upper nasal septum. Ophthalmologic evaluation showed mild left proptosis with full extraocular movements, no papilledema, and normal visual acuity. Contrast-enhanced CT of the paranasal sinuses demonstrated an expansile, mildly enhancing soft-tissue mass in the anterosuperior nasal cavity encroaching on the left orbital cavity, with remodeling of the left medial orbital wall and extension to the level of the cribriform plate, along with retention of secretions in the left frontal sinus. MRI (T1-weighted postcontrast) showed an enhancing mass reaching the nasal vault without dural enhancement or intracranial extension; T2 and non–contrast T1 sequences revealed no intratumoral hemorrhage or cystic change. The patient underwent endoscopic endonasal resection, which disclosed a cystic mass occupying the left fronto-ethmoid region with destruction of the anterior skull base and erosion of the left lamina papyracea; the dura was exposed but intact, and no cerebrospinal fluid leak was noted. A routine functional endoscopic sinus surgery was completed after tumor excision.

A. schwannoma
B. neurofibroma

A 19-year-old man with no past medical history presented with a three-week history of persistent sharp precordial pain. The pain began acutely during an episode of gastroenteritis, and gastrointestinal symptoms resolved while the chest pain remained mild and worsened on inspiration. He also noted a sporadic clicking and popping sound on the left sternal edge that could be very loud and was audible without a stethoscope; he recorded it on his smartphone. He denied shortness of breath. 

On examination, his body mass index was 18.3 kg/m2. Vital signs were normal: blood pressure within normal limits, no fever, and an oxygen saturation of 99% on room air. Lung and heart auscultation were normal except for the intermittent clicking over the left sternal border.

vignette:
A 50-year-old man with a remote history of treated Lyme disease, and no hypertension, hyperlipidemia, or diabetes, presented after four episodes of syncope over 24 hours. Six weeks earlier, he had a syncope while exercising; initial workup was unrevealing. Outpatient ECG then showed a new left bundle branch block. Exercise stress testing provoked presyncope with a brief burst of atrial tachycardia. A pharmacological nuclear stress test demonstrated an LVEF of 42% with a moderate-size area of inferior wall ischaemia and scar, but he had no chest pain or heart failure symptoms.

On current presentation, vital signs were blood pressure 140/66 mmHg, heart rate 54 bpm, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, temperature 36.2°C, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. Physical examination was unremarkable. A 12-lead ECG showed sinus rhythm at 57 bpm, first-degree AV block, and a prolonged QTc. He had a brief burst of atrial tachycardia that resolved with IV metoprolol. Cardiac enzymes, thyroid function tests, serum calcium, and ACE levels were normal. Lyme antibody testing was negative. Chest radiograph was normal. Transthoracic echocardiography showed an LVEF of 45–50% with no regional wall motion abnormalities. Telemetry captured intermittent high-grade AV block with ventricular escape beats, prompting placement of a temporary transvenous pacemaker.

Coronary angiography revealed normal coronary arteries, and left ventriculography showed an LVEF of 35–40%. A permanent dual-chamber pacemaker was implanted, and he was discharged on guideline-directed medical therapy for heart failure.

Outpatient cardiac magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated an LVEF of 31%, RV ejection fraction of 23%, and mid-myocardial late gadolinium enhancement in the basal anteroseptal wall. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the chest showed mediastinal and bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy.

vignette:
A 67-year-old woman presented with a one-month history of bleeding from the mouth, nose, and skin. Two weeks earlier, imaging had detected a splenic mass. She had no prior medical history. On examination, the spleen was not palpable. Laboratory testing revealed severe thrombocytopenia (platelet count, 1 × 10^9/L), which did not respond to recombinant human thrombopoietin, intravenous immunoglobulin, or methylprednisolone. A contrast-enhanced abdominal CT scan showed splenomegaly with a 57 × 58 mm patchy low-density lesion. In the arterial phase, the lesion exhibited moderate peripheral enhancement and central hypoenhancement; in the venous phase, there was slightly reduced enhancement centrally. vignette:
A 44-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with 2 days of sharp, stabbing right-sided chest pain (8/10) worsened by exertion and relieved by leaning forward, accompanied by shortness of breath on minimal activity. She also reported chronic right lower-leg swelling and six months of symmetric wrist stiffness that improved during the day. Her history included heavy menstrual bleeding, a miscarriage at age 14, chronic warfarin-refractory deep vein thromboses, and placement of a nonretrievable inferior vena cava filter. She denied fevers, chills, or intravenous drug use.

On examination she was obese and mildly tachypneic, sitting forward. Vital signs: temperature 98.6°F, blood pressure 116/91 mm Hg, heart rate 88/min, respiratory rate 20/min, oxygen saturation 98% on room air. She had a malar rash, jugular venous distension, tender anterior chest wall, bibasilar Velcro crackles, and a grade 2/6 pansystolic murmur at the left sternal border that increased with inspiration.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 10.2 g/dL, platelets 71 × 10^3/mm^3, ESR 55 mm/h, CRP 90.9 mg/L, D-dimer 3.7 µg/mL, and prolonged PTT of 49 s with normal PT/INR/fibrinogen. Lower-extremity duplex ultrasound was negative for DVT. Chest radiograph revealed cardiomegaly, blunting of the right costophrenic angle, and elevated bilateral hemidiaphragms. Transthoracic echocardiography showed an ejection fraction of 55–60%, moderate-to-severe tricuspid regurgitation, a 1.6 × 0.9 cm tricuspid-valve vegetation, and mild pericardial effusion. vignette:
A 78-year-old woman with a history of two prior catheter ablations for persistent atrial fibrillation—initial pulmonary vein isolation followed six months later by repeat pulmonary vein reisolation, complex fractionated electrogram ablation, and linear lesions across the left atrial roof and mitral isthmus—presented with palpitations. A 12-lead ECG during tachycardia showed an atrial cycle length of 280 ms with positive P waves in leads II, III, aVF, and V₁. An electroanatomic activation map demonstrated counterclockwise propagation around the mitral annulus and left atrial appendage, interrupted by a low-voltage scar at the prior mitral isthmus line. Entrainment pacing revealed postpacing intervals within 20 ms of the tachycardia cycle length at the inferior and lateral mitral annulus and at the left atrial appendage–left pulmonary vein ridge, but a postpacing interval more than 20 ms longer than the cycle length when pacing adjacent to the mitral isthmus scar. These findings suggested an epicardial pathway bypassing the scar. A 2F octapolar catheter was advanced into the vein of Marshall, and recordings showed activation within the vein of Marshall that matched the tachycardia cycle length.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

Options:
A. Atrial tachycardia
B. classic ridge

A 48-year-old otherwise healthy woman presented with a 5-day history of headache, nausea, and vomiting. Physical examination and laboratory tests were within normal limits. She was diagnosed with tension headache and sinusitis and discharged on trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole. Three days later, her headache had resolved but vomiting persisted twice daily; she was treated with an over-the-counter proton pump inhibitor for suspected gastroesophageal reflux. Over the following week, she developed ataxia, diplopia, and recurrence of her headache. 

She presented to the emergency department, and a T2-weighted MRI of the head showed increased signaling of the left temporal lobe, bilateral pontine regions, left peridentate nucleus, and cervical spinal cord. Neurologically, she had decreased sensorium, hallucinations, diminished attention span, and gait disturbance. A lumbar puncture showed an elevated opening pressure.

She received plasmapheresis without improvement. A follow-up T2-weighted MRI showed progressive enlargement of the bilateral pontine regions with hydrocephalus and mass effect on the fourth ventricle.
